addressed-ir005.title: A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning
addressed-ir005.summary: The Bellman variance identity must include variation across successor means.

checks.location: Lemma 3 (Wasserstein contraction) and Appendix Proposition 1 (variance contraction)
checks.claim: Appendix variance Proposition 1 claims contraction for arbitrary input distributions while its proof omits the variance of successor conditional means.
checks.explanation: The variance of the conditional mean across successor states is missing. Input distributions can have identical variances but different means, producing different mixture variances.
checks.demonstration: Let a root state transition equally to two successors \(u,v\), with reward zero. Set \(Z_1(u)=\delta_0\), \(Z_1(v)=\delta_2\), and \(Z_2=\delta_0\) everywhere. Every input variance is zero. The root output for \(Z_1\) is an equal mixture of \(0\) and \(2\gamma\), with variance \(\gamma^2\); the output for \(Z_2\) has variance zero. The asserted right side is zero, while its left side is at least \(\gamma^2>0\).
checks.repair: Under the source’s reward/transition independence convention, let \(m_Z\) and \(v_Z\) be the successor mean and variance profiles. The law of total variance gives \[\operatorname{Var}(\mathcal T^\pi Z)(x,a)=\operatorname{Var}R(x,a)+\gamma^2\{P^\pi v_Z(x,a)+\operatorname{Var}_{(X^{\prime},A^{\prime})\sim P^\pi}[m_Z(X^{\prime},A^{\prime})]\}.\] For two distributions with the same mean profile, the last terms cancel, recovering the \(\gamma^2\) contraction of variance differences. If that common profile is the Bellman fixed mean, this restricted class is invariant under the update. Section 5.4, Equation (5.19), of the authors’ Distributional Reinforcement Learning book supplies the full identity for arbitrary inputs.
checks.scope: The unrestricted variance contraction is false. The later book provides the correct transformation, not a proof of that unrestricted claim or an explicit erratum. Wasserstein contraction remains a distinct valid result.
checks.title: Bellman variance includes variation across successor means
checks.claimContext: The appendix’s Proposition 1 asserts a \(\gamma^2\) contraction between variance vectors for arbitrary input return distributions. Its proof replaces the variance of a successor-state mixture by the expected within-state variance. The paper’s separate Wasserstein contraction theorem does not make that replacement.
checks.whyItMatters: The Bellman variance identity must include variation across successor means.
checks.verificationNote: The retained whole PDF is arXiv:1707.06887v1 (uploaded 2017-07-21); its SHA-256 matches the original source record. The latest public arXiv entry names the same revision. The displayed error remains in that retained version; the repair or correct formulation is supplied by the separately identified related source. No author acknowledgement is inferred from the related source.

addressed-ir005.issueTitle: Bellman variance includes variation across successor means
addressed-ir005.plainExplanation: Equal within-state variances do not imply equal variances after mixing states with different means. The authors’ later book gives the complete total-variance identity. A variance contraction follows on a common-mean class, not for arbitrary input distributions.

addressed-io-1801-09344.summary: The printed SDP matrix misplaces a constant block; the official code uses the correct order.

checks.location: Sections3.2–3.3, especially Eq8–10: gradient/QP/SDP adversarial-score bound; Complete derivation pp3–5; Eq8 visually inspected in raghunathan_matrix.png; official author implementation read
checks.claim: Eq. (8) puts the constant block against s instead of t. Eq. (9) therefore differs from Eq. (7), and the Eq. (10) certificate can underestimate the actual score.
checks.explanation: The printed matrix actually represents \(\tfrac12(\mathbf1+t)^TAs\). This is a different optimization problem and its optimum can be smaller than the required gradient bound.
checks.demonstration: Take one hidden ReLU unit and two inputs, with \(W=(1,-1)\), \(v=1\), so \(A=(1,-1)^T\). The desired expression has maximum \(2\): choose \(s=1\), \(t=(1,-1)\). In the printed matrix, the constant block vanishes because \(\mathbf1^TA=0\), leaving \(\tfrac12s(t_1-t_2)\). Its SDP relaxation has value exactly \(1\). Indeed, positive semidefiniteness and diagonal bounds imply \(|P_{s,t_i}|\le1\), so its value is at most \(1\); the stated rank-one signs attain it. For \(x=(0.5,0.25)\), radius \(\epsilon=0.1\), and perturbation \((0.1,-0.1)\), both points lie in the unit box and the ReLU remains active. The actual score increases from \(0.25\) to \(0.45\), exceeding the printed certificate \(0.25+0.1\cdot1=0.35\).
checks.repair: With the source’s order \(y=(1,t,s)\), use \[M=\begin{pmatrix}0&(A\mathbf1)^T&0\\A\mathbf1&0&A\\0&A^T&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its quadratic form divided by four is exactly Equation (7). The PSD relaxation then upper-bounds that form because every sign vector gives a feasible rank-one matrix. The official code-bounds implementation uses the equivalent order \((1,s,t)\) and places the summed constant vector against the input-direction block \(t\), as required.
checks.scope: The displayed matrix and its printed certificate are contradicted. The separate implementation uses the correct block, so this is not evidence that its computed certificates or experiments fail.
checks.title: The SDP matrix places its constant block on the wrong coordinates
checks.claimContext: Equation (7) rewrites the gradient relaxation as \(\max_{s\in[-1,1]^m,t\in[-1,1]^d}\tfrac12t^TA(\mathbf1+s)\), where \(A=W^T\operatorname{diag}(v)\). Equation (8) packs coordinates as \(y=(1,t,s)\), but places its constant block against \(s\). Equation (10) uses the resulting SDP as an upper certificate.

Conditional orthogonality gives the exact decomposition \[\mathbb E[(X_o-g)^2]=\mathbb E[(X_o-m)^2]+\mathbb E[(g-m)^2].\] Moreover \[\mathbb E[(g-m)^2]=\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(g\mid F)]+\mathbb E[(\mathbb E[g\mid F]-m(F))^2].\] Thus equality with the local Bayes infimum requires both conditional variance and conditional bias to vanish. Drawing iid cavity fields from the correct marginal law does not itself establish that requirement. Appendix H.1 acknowledges the initialization randomness but invokes Bayes attainment by construction without proving this conditional equality. The explicit radius-one operational rule in Appendix E is described for discrete diffusion, while Theorem 1 is continuous and the precise continuous update sequencing is underspecified. checks.location: Proposition3.1; v2 PDF p.9
checks.claim:
Then any ordering $\sigma$ that
is causal and confidence based (i.e., for each $\ell\leq N$ , $\sigma(\ell+1)$ only depends on on the BP marginals of $\mu^{\sigma,\ell}_{G}$ ) has the same success probability as random ordering.
checks.explanation: With finitely many BP rounds, selecting a variable that is already forced can expose further forced variables before they are guessed. The resulting success probability differs even after exact averaging over the stated random-formula ensemble; the discrepancy is not a fixed-label or two-variable-clause artifact.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(k=3\), \(N=5\) and \(M=2\) under the paper’s independent uniform signed-clause law. Use one synchronous BP round with uniform unobserved messages. A variable is forced exactly when a clause’s other variables are revealed; otherwise its marginal is fair. The confidence policy selects a forced variable whenever one exists, using uniform ties, and otherwise selects uniformly. The comparison policy always selects uniformly among unrevealed variables. Both sample the selected BP marginal.

For two distinct three-variable clauses sharing one variable, the four other variables are leaves. Confidence-first succeeds surely. Random ordering fails only when the shared variable is last, an event of probability \(1/5\), and the two independently guessed leaf parities disagree, with probability \(1/2\). Its success is \(9/10\).

For clauses sharing two variables, ignore the fifth, isolated variable. The first two revealed variables among the four relevant ones are the two leaves with probability \(1/6\), the two shared variables with probability \(1/6\), or a mixed pair with probability \(2/3\). Their confidence-first success probabilities are \(1/2,1,1\), giving \(11/12\). For a mixed pair, uniform ordering next selects the remaining forced shared variable with probability \(1/2\); otherwise it guesses the other leaf before two-step propagation reaches it, succeeding with probability \(1/2\). Thus its mixed-case success is \(3/4\), and total success is \(3/4\). Identical variable triples have mean success \(1/2\) for both policies because their independent signs agree with probability \(1/2\).

A second uniformly sampled triple intersects the first in one, two or three variables with probabilities \(3/10,6/10,1/10\). Therefore \[P_{\mathrm{conf}}=\frac3{10}+\frac6{10}\frac{11}{12}+\frac1{10}\frac12=\frac9{10},\qquad P_{\mathrm{random}}=\frac3{10}\frac9{10}+\frac6{10}\frac34+\frac1{10}\frac12=\frac{77}{100}.\] Exact rational enumeration of all \(20^2=400\) ordered signed-clause pairs agrees. If BP is run to hard-message closure instead, both policies give \(9/10\) on this ensemble. Conditional on satisfiability the finite-round values remain different, \(18/19\) versus \(77/95\), while the closure values are both \(18/19\).
checks.repair: Specify the BP convention in Proposition 3.1. The exact equality cannot cover the stated family of finite-radius denoisers. If the intended claim concerns converged hard BP or an asymptotic regime, state that restriction, the tie rule and the probability law, and prove equality there; the finite control alone does not prove a universal replacement. On this two-clause ensemble, processing hard BP to closure yields the equal value \(9/10\), which isolates the finite-propagation issue.
checks.scope: The exact unqualified equality fails for a permitted finite-radius BP denoiser on the stated random 3-XORSAT ensemble. This is not a refutation of an explicitly converged-BP or asymptotic result, and no sampling advantage in the large-system limit is claimed.
checks.title: Finite-radius BP can give confidence ordering a different success probability
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3.1 asserts equal success probabilities for every causal ordering determined by the current BP marginals and uniform random ordering. The local denoiser uses \(r\) BP iterations. The proposition does not restrict \(N\), the number of clauses or \(r\), and does not require BP convergence. Let \(P_{\mathrm{conf}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{random}}\) denote the two success probabilities, averaged over random formulas and the algorithms’ randomness.

checks.explanation: Let \(M_{\mathrm{ID}}=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), \(M_{\mathrm{OOD}}=\operatorname{diag}(.49,.51)\). The leading projectors are orthogonal, so their Frobenius distance is \(\sqrt2\). The perturbation has norm \(.51\sqrt2\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{ID}}=1\), making the printed RHS \(1.02<\sqrt2\). Moreover its off-diagonal cross term \((I-\Pi_{\mathrm{ID}})E\Pi_{\mathrm{ID}}\) is zero, so Appendix A.1 Step 2 would incorrectly give zero rotation. A diagonal crossing changes which invariant subspace is selected without an off-diagonal coupling. A general safe global bound is \(\|P-Q\|_F\leq2\|E\|_F/\gamma_{\mathrm{ID}}\): the ID variational gap gives \(\gamma\|P-Q\|_F^2/2\leq\operatorname{tr}(M_{\mathrm{ID}}(P-Q))\leq\|E\|_F\|P-Q\|_F\), using optimality of \(Q\) for the perturbed matrix.
